whyCorrect: Match the forest to the flaw the text names for that size. The text says that in large forests the model's predictions for large-mammal populations are too high; Beaverhead-Deerlodge is explicitly a large forest at over 3 million acres. So applying the model there would produce large-mammal numbers above the real ones — it would overestimate them. The small-forest flaw is a separate condition and does not apply here.

whyWrong.A: Uses the wrong half of the text: the small-mammal flaw belongs to small forests, and it is an underestimate, not an exaggeration.
whyWrong.C: Predator-prey relationships are never mentioned; the text only describes the model's size-related errors, not what variables it leaves out.
whyWrong.D: The text says nothing about the model incorporating other factors — its stated defect is the size of the predicted population, not the range of causes it tracks.

commonMistakes: Reading 'too small' as attaching to large forests because that phrase sits closer to the end of the sentence.
tips: On inference blanks built from a two-part rule, first identify which part of the rule the specific case falls under, then carry only that part into the blank.

whyCorrect: The possessive in the blank belongs to the Nakhchivan Republic, which is one republic — singular. A singular thing takes the singular possessive its, giving "Like its peer autonomous Soviet socialist republics." The plural noun that follows the blank is what is possessed, not the possessor, so it does not control the pronoun.

whyWrong.A: Plural possessive; it would need a plural owner, but the owner is the single Nakhchivan Republic.
whyWrong.B: A contraction of they are, which puts a subject and verb where a possessive is needed: "Like they are peer republics."
whyWrong.D: A contraction of it is, not a possessive; the sentence would read "Like it is peer republics."

tips: Expand any apostrophe form aloud — if "it is" or "they are" does not fit the slot, you need the possessive spelling.

whyCorrect: Find the noun the pronoun replaces: the sentence is about how a folktale begins, and it is the folktale that is being told. That is singular, so the pronoun must be it and the verb must be present-tense is to match "depends" in the main clause. "In which it is being told" is the only pairing that gets both number and tense right.

whyWrong.A: Plural pronoun and past tense; the antecedent is the singular "a folktale" and the sentence is in the present.
whyWrong.B: "These" has no plural antecedent in the sentence, and it points to nothing specific.
whyWrong.C: Right tense but wrong number — "they" cannot refer back to the singular "a folktale."

commonMistakes: Letting the plural sense of "folktales in general" override the actual singular noun printed in the sentence.

whyCorrect: Test each side of the blank. "In Norway, the Longyearbyen observatory site monitors activity in the upper atmosphere of the northern hemisphere" is a complete sentence, and "in Australia, another observatory site, Buckland Park, monitors the sky of the southern hemisphere" is also complete. Two independent clauses need a semicolon (or a period), so hemisphere; is the only option that joins them legally.

whyWrong.A: "And" without a preceding comma still runs two independent clauses together; a coordinating conjunction joining full clauses needs a comma before it.
whyWrong.B: No punctuation at all creates a fused sentence.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

tips: Cover the blank and read each side on its own — if both sides can stand alone, a comma is never enough.

whyCorrect: "Between 2006 and 2012" is an introductory prepositional phrase, not a clause, so it needs only a comma before the subject that follows. That gives "Between 2006 and 2012, these lions prowled the Greater Kruger National Park game reserve," a complete sentence with "these lions" as subject and "prowled" as verb.

whyWrong.A: "When" turns the rest into a subordinate clause, so the sentence never reaches a main verb and ends as a fragment.
whyWrong.B: A period leaves "Between 2006 and 2012" standing alone as a fragment with no subject or verb.
whyWrong.C: "Because" subordinates the only clause that could serve as the main clause, again leaving a fragment.

commonMistakes: Assuming a date range is long enough to be a sentence; it is still just a phrase.

whyCorrect: The title "A Tear" identifies which hit song is meant, so it is essential to the noun and takes no punctuation before it: "you would have heard the hit song 'A Tear' by Gene McDaniels." Punctuation here would cut the noun off from the words that specify it.

whyWrong.A: A colon must follow a complete sentence, and "chances are you would have heard the hit song" leaves the verb's object dangling.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; what follows it here is only a title and a byline.
whyWrong.C: A comma would mark the title as nonessential extra information, but without it the reader does not know which song is meant.

tips: If removing the phrase would leave the reader asking "which one?", it is essential and gets no comma.

whyCorrect: "By being passed down through private libraries" is a prepositional phrase explaining how the manuscript survived, not a clause. A phrase attaches directly to the sentence in front of it with no punctuation, so the sentence reads "...have survived from roughly the sixteenth century to the present day by being passed down through private libraries."

whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and "by being passed down..." has no subject or finite verb.
whyWrong.C: A period creates the same problem — "By being passed down through private libraries in the city of Timbuktu, Mali" is a fragment.
whyWrong.D: Placing a comma after "by" splits the preposition from its object, which no convention allows.

commonMistakes: Hearing a pause after "day" and reaching for punctuation, when the phrase that follows is grammatically part of the same clause.

whyCorrect: Read what the blank actually modifies: "_____ years pass between a soil's selection and official designation, as the legislative process can be notoriously slow." The clause needs a word telling you how frequently that delay happens, and the reason given — a slow legislature — supports a general statement of frequency. Often supplies exactly that.

whyWrong.A: Signals a conclusion drawn from the previous sentence, but two designation dates do not logically cause the delay claim.
whyWrong.C: Signals a comparison to a like case; this sentence introduces a new general point rather than paralleling the examples.
whyWrong.D: Confirms or intensifies a claim already made, and nothing before the blank asserts that the process takes years.

tips: When the blank sits before a noun like "years," check whether the slot wants a frequency word rather than a logical connector.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a general rule: sleek vehicles are more aerodynamic than bulky ones. The sentence with the blank then names a specific sleek vehicle, the T-45 Goshawk, and a specific bulky one, a pickup truck. That relationship is illustration, so the parenthetical transition must be for instance.

whyWrong.A: Signals that two things happen at the same time or shifts to a separate situation; the jet is not a separate situation but a case of the rule just stated.
whyWrong.B: Signals contrast, but the jet example agrees with the general rule rather than complicating it.
whyWrong.D: Signals an added, separate point, yet nothing new is being added — the same claim is being demonstrated.

tips: When a sentence names a specific instance of the claim just made, the transition is almost always an example signal.

whyCorrect: Track the time frame. The first sentence is about 1889, when the tower's silhouette was attacked as a novelty; the second says the same design now turns up everywhere from Rio to Copenhagen. The shift is from the past to the present, so a time transition is what the blank needs, and Nowadays supplies it.

whyWrong.A: Introduces a correction of a preceding claim, but the text is not denying that the design was once criticized — it is describing a later state of affairs.
whyWrong.B: Signals a summary of points already made; a new fact about the design's current spread is not a conclusion.
whyWrong.C: Signals an additional supporting point, but the second sentence reverses the situation rather than reinforcing it.

commonMistakes: Grabbing a contrast word because the two sentences feel opposed, when the opposition is really then-versus-now.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is to identify the sculpture, so the sentence must name it. Only the choice that includes the title Sculpture Classique alongside the prize does that. It also keeps Arp as the winner, so nothing needed for the goal is missing.

whyWrong.A: Says only "a sculpture" and never names it, so the identification the goal demands is exactly what is left out.
whyWrong.B: Names the awarding museum and the year but not the sculpture.
whyWrong.D: Explains what the Carnegie Prize is; it never mentions Arp's work at all.

tips: For notes questions, underline the goal's key noun — here "the sculpture" — and eliminate every choice that does not contain it.

whyCorrect: "How long" means the sentence has to give both endpoints of the escudo's use. The notes supply them: adopted in 1914, replaced in 1980. Stating "from 1914 to 1980" lets the reader compute the span directly, which no other choice allows.

whyWrong.A: Reports that a replacement happened but gives no dates at all, so the duration cannot be determined.
whyWrong.B: Gives only the 1914 start date and never says when the escudo stopped being official.
whyWrong.D: Gives the metical's span rather than the escudo's; it tells you when the escudo ended but not when it began.

commonMistakes: Picking the choice that mentions both currencies, when the goal only asks about the escudo's own time in use.

whyCorrect: The goal is a similarity, so the sentence must state something true of both programs at once. The notes give a shared trait: both are slow TV documentaries covering ordinary events in real time. The choice that puts both titles under that single description is the only one that emphasizes what they have in common.

whyWrong.A: Describes one program only, so no comparison of any kind is made.
whyWrong.B: Names both programs but sets their subjects side by side as different things, which emphasizes contrast rather than similarity.
whyWrong.C: Compares their running times to point out a difference in length, the opposite of the stated goal.

commonMistakes: Treating any sentence that mentions both programs as a similarity statement, even when the connecting word is "while" or "compared to."

whyCorrect: The second sentence is the definition of the blank: scholars "may inadvertently overlook nuances" by attending only to the obvious movement-level features. The blank therefore needs a word meaning to treat subtleties as unimportant, and discount means exactly that.

whyWrong.B: Means to examine closely — the reverse of overlooking the subtleties.
whyWrong.C: Means to enlarge or intensify, but the problem described is that the subtleties get missed, not blown up.
whyWrong.D: Means to condemn openly, which is a deliberate public criticism rather than the inadvertent oversight the text describes.

tips: When the sentence after the blank restates the same idea, treat it as a definition and find the synonym.

whyCorrect: Both verbs describe Gogol putting his name on things: he cuts it into clay with paper clips and puts his signature under paintings in brush strokes. The one meaning that fits both actions is making a mark on a surface. Substitute "marks his name into the bottoms" and "marks his signature below paintings" and the sense holds.

whyWrong.B: "Leaves" can mean departs or passes by, but that reading makes nonsense of carving a name into clay.
whyWrong.C: "Carves" can suggest turning or shaping wood, yet nothing here is being rotated or converted.
whyWrong.D: "Follows" would describe going after something, which neither verb does in these sentences.

commonMistakes: Choosing a meaning that works for one of the two verbs; the question requires a single sense that fits both.

whyCorrect: The designers want people to interact with robots comfortably, so a human-like feature such as walking on two legs must be working against the unnatural aspects of the robot's look. The blank needs a word meaning to lessen or soften that effect, and ameliorate carries that sense. The "but" clause confirms it by describing what happens when this softening goes too far.

whyWrong.B: Means to merge into one mass; features do not fuse the unnatural aspects together, and that would not help interaction.
whyWrong.C: Means to increase, which would make the unnatural aspects more noticeable — the opposite of the design goal.
whyWrong.D: Means to prove or confirm with evidence, which cannot apply to an effect on how a robot looks.

tips: When a design is described as solving a problem, the verb in the blank almost always means reduce, not add.

whyCorrect: The only detail the sentence gives about the mosque is scale: it is "massive" and holds roughly 30,000 people. The blank must therefore describe the impression that sheer size makes on a viewer, and imposing means grand and impressive because of size. The other options describe qualities the sentence never establishes.

whyWrong.A: Means not real or deceptive, but nothing suggests the mosque only appears to be there.
whyWrong.B: Means treated as perfect or better than reality; the sentence reports actual capacity, not an idealized version.
whyWrong.C: Means elaborately detailed, which is a claim about ornament rather than about size, and no detail work is described.

tips: Pick the word that matches the evidence actually given in the sentence, not a word that would sound good about a building in general.

whyCorrect: Two clues fix the blank. The program identified sidewalks "in the vast majority of cases" and even distinguished concrete from cobblestone, and the last sentence calls this an "already strong performance." The blank must be positive and about consistent accuracy, which is what reliably means.

whyWrong.B: Means awkwardly or ineptly, contradicting the description of strong performance.
whyWrong.C: Means seldom, which flatly contradicts "the vast majority of cases."
whyWrong.D: Speed is never discussed; the passage measures how often the program was right, not how long it took.

commonMistakes: Assuming a negative word fits because the sentence mentions testing, when the surrounding text praises the results.

whyCorrect: Walk the text in order. It names Karuk and then Haida as isolates, then contrasts them with most Native languages, which belong to families. It closes by noting that isolates are actually most common in regions full of nonisolates and suggesting the same geographical circumstances drive both — a point where the two categories correspond rather than differ.

whyWrong.B: The text never describes nonisolates evolving out of isolates; a family descends from a single shared ancestor language, which is a different claim.
whyWrong.C: It says isolates and nonisolates turn up in the same regions, so the text does not distinguish between their regions.
whyWrong.D: No nonisolate language is ever named, and the similarity is proposed at the end, not in the middle.

tips: For structure questions, check the order of the moves as well as their content — a choice can list real ideas in the wrong sequence.

whyCorrect: The text opens by naming Cardelús and her subject, spends the middle explaining what canopy soil is and how it forms, and closes by tying that back to why she studies it in Costa Rica. That is a straightforward introduce-then-explain structure with no argument in it.

whyWrong.B: No idea is disputed; Cardelús is presented as studying canopy soil, not as opposing a claim.
whyWrong.C: Only one kind of tree is mentioned, and no sizes are tracked over time.
whyWrong.D: There is no disagreement between researchers — only one researcher appears in the text.

commonMistakes: Expecting every structure question to involve a conflict, and so choosing a choice that invents one.

whyCorrect: Trace the path of each word. Coyote travelled Nahuatl to Spanish to English, and condor travelled Quechua to Spanish to English. In both cases Spanish is the middle step that carried an Indigenous word into English, so the point about Spanish is that it acted as the channel for that influence.

whyWrong.B: The text never counts or compares how much vocabulary each source contributed to English.
whyWrong.C: Spanish is only shown borrowing from Indigenous languages; nothing says it gave words back to them.
whyWrong.D: Two examples are given, one from each language, which says nothing about the overall numbers Spanish adopted.

tips: When a text traces the same route twice, the point being made is usually about the shared middle step.

whyCorrect: The text says Davis and Evans "omitted parts, such as the aria 'I Got Plenty of Nuthin','" and the parts they omitted come from Gershwin's 1935 opera. So the aria belongs to the original opera and was left out of the 1958 adaptation. The correct choice is the one that places it in Gershwin's work rather than in the adaptation.

whyWrong.B: The "brief gestures toward Gershwin's melodies" describe other material; this aria is named as one of the omissions, so no quotation of it survives.
whyWrong.C: Listener reaction to this specific aria is never reported — the text only says Davis and Evans did not aim to satisfy listeners wanting an exact duplication.
whyWrong.D: Milestones is named only as a Davis album; nothing connects it to this aria or to the Gershwin adaptation.

commonMistakes: Blurring "they made brief gestures toward Gershwin's melodies" into a claim about the one item the text explicitly says was cut.

whyCorrect: Separate the narrator's two claims. He says Hans Castorp is "a perfectly ordinary, if engaging young man" and that the story is told for its own sake because it is "very much worth telling" — an extraordinary story about an ordinary man. The parenthetical then concedes a point in Hans's favor: it is his story, and "not every story happens to everybody," which is precisely the argument that the story's worth reflects back on him.

whyWrong.A: Reverses the narrator, who says the story is worth telling for its own sake, not that all people are inherently interesting; and he never says time makes its interest hard to grasp.
whyWrong.B: Treats the story's age and required past tense as evidence of importance, but the narrator asserts the story's worth independently and mentions age only to explain the tense.
whyWrong.D: Generalizes to "all stories about inconsequential people" and claims the manner of telling is what reveals the story's significance; the narrator uses the deep past tense simply because the events are old.

tips: In dense nineteenth- and twentieth-century prose, the material inside dashes and parentheses is usually where the concession the question tests is hidden.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that a late arrival of subfreezing temperatures helps invasives more than natives. Support therefore has to compare the two species in exactly those late-onset years and show the invasive gaining more. The finding that both species extended leaf production in late-onset years but that the extension was much larger for the invasive P. aviculare than for the native V. edule is that comparison.

whyWrong.B: Reports no change in leaf production despite varying onset dates, which shows the delay has no effect on either species and so supports nothing.
whyWrong.C: Has the invasive stopping producing leaves sooner in late-onset years, which would mean the delay disadvantages it.
whyWrong.D: Adds an early spring start to the same years, so any gain cannot be attributed to the autumn delay, and it reports no difference between the two species anyway.

commonMistakes: Accepting a finding that shows a change in both species without checking which species changed more — the conclusion is comparative.

whyCorrect: The research question has two variables: perceived similarity between the two categories in a pair, and likelihood of buying the extension. The team already has the second one — the change in purchase probability they computed for each pair. What is missing is a measure of how similar consumers think the two categories are, so the design must collect similarity ratings for each pair and correlate them with the probabilities already in hand.

whyWrong.B: Rates one product against others in its own category, which measures within-category similarity; the question is about similarity between the two categories in the pair.
whyWrong.C: Measures brand recognition rather than category similarity, and correlates it with purchase frequency instead of the change in probability the team calculated.
whyWrong.D: Measures brand recognition against price, so neither variable in the research question is tested.

tips: Name the two variables in the research question first, then keep only the design that measures both of them.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: Mrs. Sommers is deeply absorbed, and what absorbs her is deciding how to spend the money. The quotation about the "question of investment" occupying her greatly and her walking about "absorbed in speculation and calculation" delivers both — the deliberation and the intensity of it.

whyWrong.B: Describes her practiced technique for holding her place at a counter, which is about shopping habits, not about weighing how to spend the money.
whyWrong.C: Shows a moment at the hosiery counter after she is already shopping; it illustrates her reaction to the goods, not her deliberation over the sum.
whyWrong.D: Conveys how large the money feels and the importance it gives her, but says nothing about deciding how to spend it.

commonMistakes: Choosing a quotation about the money itself when the claim is specifically about the decision-making process.

whyCorrect: Read what the paleoecological record actually shows: clams got larger and more productive at the same time that garden practices spread and harvesting pressure rose. Normally heavier harvesting would shrink a population, so clams thriving under it points to the gardening technique keeping the food source going. The songs are what preserve that technique, so the finding supports the idea that the practice they describe worked as sustainable management.

whyWrong.A: Requires the people to have eaten less clam at times, but the text says harvesting pressure increased, not that it was periodically eased.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text traces where the practice came from; other Indigenous groups are mentioned only for their own songs, not as a source of clam gardening.
whyWrong.D: Makes a claim about present-day practice, while the evidence cited is an ancient paleoecological record.

tips: When a finding pairs a rise in pressure with a rise in yield, the inference is almost always that the management technique is effective.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets up a specific error: the novel is "largely pure invention," and some readers ignore that and keep hunting for real-life counterparts. If most of the book is invented, those extra matches they find will not actually hold, so what they risk is asserting links between the novel and Vuong's life that the evidence does not support.

whyWrong.B: Reverses the risk — these readers are overstating the real-world basis, not downplaying it; the text already grants that autobiographical parallels exist.
whyWrong.C: Readership numbers are never discussed anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.D: Concerns influence from other writers, but the text is about matching characters and events to Vuong's own life.

commonMistakes: Picking the choice that repeats the text's concession about real parallels instead of the one that names the danger of pushing that reading too far.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its verb: the rover "spent over fourteen years." The idiom is spend time doing something, so the blank takes the bare -ing form. "Spent over fourteen years collecting data" completes it without adding a second, competing verb.

whyWrong.A: Adds a second finite verb, giving "the rover spent ... is collecting," and the present tense clashes with the past-tense narration.
whyWrong.C: Also supplies a finite verb, and "were" is plural while the subject "the rover" is singular.
whyWrong.D: Produces two past-tense verbs in a row, "spent ... collected," with no conjunction joining them.

tips: If the sentence already has a main verb, the blank almost certainly needs a nonfinite form.

whyCorrect: "By supplying grain, textiles, and tin to societies that lacked these valuable items" is a long introductory modifying phrase, not a sentence — it has no subject of its own. The main clause "the Neo-Assyrian Empire grew not only in wealth but also in power and influence" follows, and an introductory phrase is set off from its main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A period leaves the introductory phrase standing as a fragment.
whyWrong.B: No punctuation at all runs the modifier straight into the subject, so the reader cannot tell where the modifier ends.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence on each side, and the material before it is only a phrase.

commonMistakes: Treating length as a sign of independence — a phrase beginning with "By supplying" can run for a full line and still be a fragment.

whyCorrect: Strip the sentence to its bones: the three named researchers are the subject and the blank holds the verb, "compiled climate data from several sites." A subject is never separated from its own verb by punctuation, so the blank takes no mark at all. The long list of names does not change that.

whyWrong.A: A comma between the subject and its verb is not permitted, however long the subject is.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but here the material before it lacks a verb entirely.
whyWrong.D: A colon must follow a complete sentence, and "researchers Martha A. Scholl, Maoya Bassiouni, and Angel J. Torres-Sánchez" is only a noun phrase.

tips: When a subject is a long list of names, cover the list and check whether the remaining skeleton is just subject plus verb.

whyCorrect: The blank refers back to Creek Council Tree and Cimarron Iron Bridge, two paintings, so the pronoun must be plural and the verb must agree with it. "In 2023, they were displayed alongside other works by Echohawk" matches that plural antecedent and keeps the passive construction intact.

whyWrong.B: Singular "this" cannot stand for two paintings, and it points vaguely at no specific noun.
whyWrong.C: Singular "it" has no singular antecedent — the previous sentence names two works.
whyWrong.D: "Some" implies an unspecified subset of a larger group, but only two specific paintings are under discussion and both are meant.

commonMistakes: Letting the singular exhibition title next to the blank pull the pronoun into the singular.

whyCorrect: Find the main verb before filling the blank: it is "consist" at the end of the sentence, whose subject is "Disyllabic words." That means the blank cannot hold another conjugated verb — it needs a past participle opening a modifier: "Disyllabic words classified as trochees ... consist of one stressed syllable followed by one unstressed syllable."

whyWrong.A: Supplies a complete verb phrase, so the sentence ends up with two main verbs, "have been classified" and "consist," and no conjunction.
whyWrong.B: Same problem — "can be classified" is a finite verb phrase, leaving "consist" stranded.
whyWrong.C: Also finite; "words are classified ... consist" is ungrammatical.

tips: Read past a long interrupting phrase to the end of the sentence — the verb waiting there tells you the blank must be a modifier.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its main verb, "ensured," whose subject is "A plano-convex lens." The blank must therefore begin a modifying phrase describing what the lens does, and because the lens acts on the laser, the active participle focusing is required: "A plano-convex lens focusing the laser on the center of the crystal ensured a spot size of 85 micrometers."

whyWrong.A: As a past participle it would mean the lens itself was focused, reversing who acts on what, and read as a past-tense verb it collides with "ensured."
whyWrong.B: A finite present-tense verb, which both duplicates the main verb and clashes with the past-tense "ensured."
whyWrong.D: A finite plural verb, but the subject "lens" is singular, and the sentence again ends up with two verbs.

commonMistakes: Picking a past-tense verb because the rest of the sentence is in the past, without noticing "ensured" is already doing that job.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank makes a loose claim — that "a number" of the 206 parades honored aviation. The sentence after it sharpens that into an exact figure, 16 parades for pilots, with Corrigan's among them. Indeed is the transition for confirming and intensifying a claim just made.

whyWrong.A: Signals a separate additional point, but the second sentence restates the first one more precisely rather than adding something new.
whyWrong.B: Signals a consequence, and the count of aviation parades is not caused by the previous statement.
whyWrong.D: Signals contrast, yet the two sentences agree completely.

tips: A vague quantity followed by an exact one is a confirmation, not an addition.

whyCorrect: The two sentences put distances side by side: the JWST sits nearly a million miles past Earth's orbit, while Hubble sits about 340 miles above the surface. Those figures differ by orders of magnitude, so the blank has to mark the opposition — By contrast.

whyWrong.A: Claims the Hubble's altitude follows from the JWST's position, but the two placements are independent facts.
whyWrong.B: Signals likeness, and a million miles versus 340 miles is the opposite of alike.
whyWrong.D: Signals the second item in a list, but the sentence is not enumerating steps or points.

commonMistakes: Reading both sentences as "facts about telescopes" and reaching for an addition word instead of noticing the numbers are being set against each other.

whyCorrect: The pattern described first is brood parasitism: females visit dozens of nests and leave eggs for other ducks to incubate. Subject 7F64B does the reverse on both counts — few nests, and she incubates her own eggs. The blank must therefore mark a departure from the pattern, and alternatively is the only option that does.

whyWrong.A: Would present 7F64B as an instance of the behavior just described, but she does not display it.
whyWrong.B: Would single out one member of the group just described as especially representative; 7F64B is the exception.
whyWrong.C: Signals matching behavior, which flatly contradicts what she does.

tips: Compare the specific case to the general pattern feature by feature before choosing — here both features are reversed.

whyCorrect: The goal names two disadvantages, one per plant, so the sentence must carry both. The notes give flash steam (Wairakei) a temperature requirement above 180°C that limits where it can be used, and binary cycle (Traunreut) higher maintenance costs. Only the choice that says the Traunreut system escapes the temperature limit but costs more to maintain puts both drawbacks in one comparison.

whyWrong.A: Gives only the flash steam system's temperature drawback and never mentions any downside at Traunreut.
whyWrong.B: Gives only the binary cycle's cost drawback and never mentions the temperature limitation.
whyWrong.D: States the temperature capability of each system as a neutral difference, and says nothing about cost, so no disadvantage of the Traunreut system appears.

tips: When a goal says "compare the disadvantages," the answer must contain a drawback for each side, not one drawback plus a neutral fact.

whyCorrect: "Format" means the poem's structural form — how it is built. The notes say directly that the poem is written as a sequence of seven haiku, and only one choice reports that. Everything else in the notes is about publication, theme, or the poet's reasons.

whyWrong.A: Gives Sanchez's motivation for choosing the form, not a description of the form itself.
whyWrong.B: Describes where the poem appeared and what the collection is about, which is context rather than format.
whyWrong.C: Generalizes to every poem in the book, which the notes never claim, and drops the specific poem the goal names.

commonMistakes: Accepting a choice that mentions haiku somewhere, without checking that it describes this poem's structure.

whyCorrect: An "implication" is what the find means for the existing idea. The Saltville tools are about 16,000 years old, which is older than the Clovis arrival at 13,000 years, so they indicate people were in North America before the Clovis. Stating that against the Clovis First hypothesis is what spells out the implication.

whyWrong.A: Only restates what the Clovis First hypothesis claims and never mentions the Saltville find.
whyWrong.B: Locates Saltville among other pre-Clovis sites but never says what its tools imply about the hypothesis.
whyWrong.C: Asserts that the tools have important implications without ever saying what those implications are.

tips: A choice that announces something is significant is not the same as a choice that explains the significance.

whyCorrect: The dash introduces proof of what the blank claims: visitors to Los Angeles Union Station "can easily recognize" the Spanish mission influence in its style. The blank therefore needs a word meaning plainly noticeable, and palpable means so obvious it can almost be touched.

whyWrong.B: Means downplayed or barely expressed, which contradicts an influence anyone can easily recognize.
whyWrong.C: Means challenged or in doubt, but no disagreement about the influence appears anywhere in the sentence.
whyWrong.D: Means confirmed by supporting evidence, which describes a claim's status, not how visible an architectural influence is across a state.

tips: When a dash or colon follows the blank, the material after it is usually a direct restatement of the missing word.

whyCorrect: The sentence is built on a contrast: "Although" the films had something at first, their critical standing is "now more secure," and the 2018 praise shows the current favorable view. If the reputation is only now secure, what they met at release must have been criticism, so the blank needs a word for people who disparage — detractors.

whyWrong.A: People who work with a filmmaker, which says nothing about reputation and would not contrast with later acclaim.
whyWrong.B: People who copy a work; being imitated would signal early influence, not the poor standing the contrast requires.
whyWrong.C: Things that come before, but the films themselves are what is being judged, and precursors would not affect critics' esteem.

commonMistakes: Skipping over "Although" and choosing a neutral or positive word, when the structure demands something negative before the blank's clause turns.

whyCorrect: The colon gives the data that defines the blank: a country open to foreign capital had a 0.20 chance of a swap line, a restrictive one only 0.03. A near sevenfold gap means the policy environment made a real difference to the decision, so the blank needs a phrase meaning significant or relevant to it — material to.

whyWrong.A: Not the standard idiom (the phrase is "predicated on"), and it would also reverse the direction, making the policy environment depend on the swap-line decisions.
whyWrong.B: Means unconnected, which is exactly what the 0.20-versus-0.03 gap rules out.
whyWrong.D: Reverses the relationship — it would say the swap-line decisions shaped the policy environments, not that the environments mattered to the decisions.

tips: With paired probabilities after a colon, first ask whether they show a connection or its absence, then check that the phrase points in the right causal direction.

whyCorrect: The only evidence the sentence offers is scale: the mosque is "massive" and holds about 17,000 people at once. The blank has to name the impression that size creates in a viewer, and imposing means impressive because of great size.

whyWrong.A: Means made to seem better than reality, but the sentence reports the mosque's actual capacity.
whyWrong.B: Means finely detailed, a claim about ornamentation that the sentence never makes.
whyWrong.C: Means deceptive or unreal, which contradicts a building described as physically massive.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word that sounds complimentary about architecture generally instead of the one the stated evidence — capacity — supports.

whyCorrect: The colon defines the blank: the source "has no direct bearing on whether the claim is true." A thing with no bearing on the question at hand is irrelevant to it. The first half of the sentence sets up the contrast — people treat the source as decisive, but logically it is beside the point.

whyWrong.A: Means implied rather than stated; the source of a claim is out in the open, and implicitness has nothing to do with truth.
whyWrong.B: Means impossible to question, which would make the source matter enormously — the opposite of having no bearing.
whyWrong.C: Means blurry or hard to make out, but the problem is not that the source is unclear.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, translate the clause after it into one word before you look at the choices.

whyCorrect: The first part reports what the team found: the ants detect infected wounds and treat them with antimicrobial secretions, cutting mortality by 90%. The last clause then looks forward — the researchers hope the discovery will help develop new antibiotics for people. That is a summary of findings followed by a direction for future work.

whyWrong.A: No problem is posed for the researchers to solve; the ants' own behavior is the finding, not a proposal by the team.
whyWrong.B: Evolution is never discussed — the text says what the ants do, not how the ability arose.
whyWrong.D: No methods are described; the text reports results, not how the study was conducted.

commonMistakes: Reading the ants' wound treatment as the "solution" in a problem-solution structure, when it is part of what the study found.

whyCorrect: Follow the text's movement: Spanish-language newspapers flourished across Texas, San Antonio produced eleven, El Paso outdid every city with twenty-two, and its border location and large Spanish-speaking population explain why. The whole passage builds toward that single point about the state and its standout city.

whyWrong.A: Present-day newspapers are never mentioned; every fact belongs to 1890-1900.
whyWrong.C: No influence of El Paso's papers on San Antonio's is claimed — the two cities are compared only by count.
whyWrong.D: Popularity in Mexico is never discussed; Mexico appears only to explain El Paso's location and population.

tips: The purpose statement has to cover the whole text — a choice that fits only the El Paso sentences is too narrow, and one that adds unmentioned places or times is too wide.

whyCorrect: Yung contrasts two versions of the city directly. In 1847 it held only 250,000 to 300,000 people; by 1909 it rivals London in population, wealth, and commerce, with Manhattan filled with skyscrapers, churches, and grand residences. Both halves of that contrast point the same way — more people and more building.

whyWrong.B: Yung calls the new buildings "palatial" and lists skyscrapers and churches admiringly; he never judges them as plainer or less appealing.
whyWrong.C: Politics is not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
whyWrong.D: London is invoked only as a benchmark for population, wealth, and commerce; diversity is never compared.

commonMistakes: Reading the mention of London as a claim about New York's residents rather than as a measure of the city's size and prosperity.

whyCorrect: Two details combine. Singapore is given as an example of a tax haven, and Zucman found tax havens are "rarely used by investors living in Japan" while many users live in Saudi Arabia or Greece. Put together, a Japan-based investor is less likely than a Saudi-based one to keep wealth in a haven such as Singapore.

whyWrong.A: Robeyns disapproves of tax-haven use even though it is legal, so she would not call it beneficial — and this is her view, not Zucman's research anyway.
whyWrong.C: Risk and return are never discussed, and residents of Singapore are mentioned only as the people tax havens do not serve.
whyWrong.D: Reverses the finding: Japan is where havens are rarely used, and Greece is where many users live.

tips: When a text names an example of a category early on, expect a choice later to swap the example in for the category — track that Singapore stands for "tax haven."

whyCorrect: The claim has a specific shape: an expected, widespread shift in what the public does, which cultured meat could answer. A quotation about a growing population eating significantly more meat and driving up demand through the century is a forecast about mass behavior, and since cultured meat is meat produced without livestock, it directly addresses that rising demand.

whyWrong.A: Compares water use between lab-grown and conventional meat, which is an environmental argument, not a prediction about public behavior.
whyWrong.B: Explains what makes meat taste different across species and farming conditions, which has nothing to do with future behavior.
whyWrong.D: Reports a current consumer belief about packaging, not an anticipated change in behavior, and packaging is unrelated to cultured meat.

commonMistakes: Choosing the quotation that praises cultured meat, when the claim requires evidence of the behavior change rather than of the product's merits.

whyCorrect: "Mixed feelings" means one quotation has to hold both a positive and a negative reaction to the same surroundings. Only the line "I'm really getting quite fond of the big room, all but that horrid [wall]paper" does that: fondness for the room, revulsion at the paper, in a single sentence.

whyWrong.A: Calls the sub-pattern "particularly irritating" — wholly negative, with nothing favorable alongside it.
whyWrong.B: Observes that the paper looks different by moonlight, which is a change in appearance rather than a feeling of any kind.
whyWrong.D: Piles up negatives — "repellant," "almost revolting," "unclean" — so there is no positive side to mix.

tips: For a "mixed" or "conflicted" claim, scan for a single quotation containing a turn word such as "but" or "all but."

whyCorrect: Pin down what the conclusion claims: anatomy affects the ability to tell speech from nonspeech. Support therefore has to sort dogs by a physical feature and compare how sharply each group separated the two languages from the scrambled recording. The finding that shorter-headed dogs showed less of a gap than longer-headed dogs between real speech and the scrambled audio does exactly that.

whyWrong.A: Compares long-headed dogs on the scrambled recording against short-headed dogs on a familiar language, so the groups differ in two ways at once and nothing can be attributed to anatomy.
whyWrong.B: Compares two sets of long-headed dogs by which language they knew, holding anatomy constant, so it tests familiarity rather than head shape.
whyWrong.D: Sorts by anatomy but measures familiar versus unfamiliar language, which is language recognition, not the speech-versus-nonspeech distinction the conclusion names.

tips: Write the conclusion as "variable X affects outcome Y," then reject any finding that does not vary X while measuring Y.

whyCorrect: The team set out to decide among culture, personal taste, and anatomy. What they observed is that ten groups with very different ways of living rated odors about the same, with peach-scented ethyl butyrate beating garlicky diethyl disulfide across the board. Agreement across cultures is evidence against culture being the driver, so the idea the study undermines is that culture significantly shapes odor preference.

whyWrong.A: Misstates the result — the study found that different people rank the same odors similarly, not that one person rates all pleasant odors equally.
whyWrong.C: The study's cross-cultural agreement leaves room for individual variation and does not undercut a claim about personal taste.
whyWrong.D: States what the results actually support, so the study reinforces it rather than undermining it.

commonMistakes: Picking the option that matches the finding instead of the one the finding refutes — the sentence asks what was undermined.

whyCorrect: The blank has to follow from the reason just given: gold was much rarer than bronze. If gold was scarce, then not every buried hoard would contain any, and the text has already named a second hoard, Parc-y-Meirch, without ever attributing gold to it. So the unsurprising consequence is that some hoards, that one included, held no gold.

whyWrong.B: Melting and reuse is a separate practice the text never raises, and rarity alone does not establish that gold objects were recycled.
whyWrong.C: Talks about transferring metalworking skills from bronze to gold, which scarcity of gold does not explain.
whyWrong.D: Concerns how hoards came to be found, but the reason given is about how much gold existed, not about excavation.

tips: When the blank follows "thus it is not surprising that," the answer must be the direct consequence of the clause immediately before it.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences: "Gitlin's use of the term referenced TV studios' practice of repackaging successful narrative formulas as new content" and "even shows that varied only slightly from other shows still attracted sizeable audiences." They need a semicolon between them, and "in that era" then works as an introductory phrase on the second clause, followed by its own comma.

whyWrong.A: Leaves only commas between two independent clauses, producing a splice no matter where "in that era" is placed.
whyWrong.B: Also joins two independent clauses with a comma alone.
whyWrong.C: Same splice, and it additionally strands "in that era" without the closing comma its position requires.

tips: Decide the clause boundary first, then place the short phrase — the punctuation joining the clauses is what the question is really testing.

whyCorrect: The long list of gods is an interrupter opened with an em dash after "pantheon," and an interrupter must close with the same mark it opened with. Inside the list the items are already separated by semicolons because each contains its own comma, so the blank's job is only to end the interruption and hand the sentence back to "may have been historical figures." An em dash after Crius does that.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon would signal another list item is coming, but the list is finished and the main clause resumes.
whyWrong.C: A comma is too weak to close a dash-opened interrupter, and it also mimics the internal punctuation of the list items.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the list runs straight into the verb, so the reader never learns the interruption has ended.

commonMistakes: Continuing the semicolon pattern through the final item instead of noticing the dash that opened the whole list.
